name: Design an Online Auction System
intent: Let millions of people bid on items so that every bid is checked against the latest price, the highest bidder always wins, late bids cannot steal the auction, watchers see each change at once, and each auction closes exactly once.
codeTitle: versioned bids with proxy bidding, extension and an exactly-once close
finalIntro: One bid arriving in the last two minutes of an auction, and the auction closing.
prompt: Design the bidding part of an online marketplace. Sellers list items with a start price and an end time. Buyers place bids, and can give a maximum so that the system bids for them. The highest bidder when the auction ends wins and is charged. Thousands of people may watch one popular auction, and many bid in its last minutes.
functional: Place a bid, with an optional maximum that the system defends automatically (proxy bidding)
Accept a bid only if it beats the current price by the minimum increment
Show the current price and leader to everyone watching, as it changes
Extend the end time when a bid arrives in the final minutes
Close each auction at its end time, pick the winner and create one order
Keep a complete, tamper-evident history of bids
nonFunctional: Never accept two bids that both think they beat the same price
A bid is confirmed or rejected within about 200 ms, even on a hot auction
Watchers see a new price within about a second
Each auction closes exactly once, within a few seconds of its end time, and survives crashes
Handle the final-minute surge on popular items without slowing other auctions
Be fair: the same rules for everyone, based on the server's clock, and detect shill and bot bidding

firstAttempt.text: One bids table. A bid does a read of the highest bid, checks that the new amount is higher, and inserts a row. Watchers poll the page every few seconds. A cron job every minute finds auctions whose end time has passed, takes the highest bid and sends the winner an order.
limits: Two bidders read the same price and both insert, so two bids both think they won, and the check no longer means anything
Polling by thousands of watchers hammers the database on exactly the auctions that matter most
A bid placed one second before the end gives the other bidder no time to answer, so sniping decides the winner
The cron job can run twice, or crash halfway, and then the winner is charged twice or not at all
Bidders must keep guessing how much to bid, and the table has no record of why a price changed

steps.title: Make every bid a conditional write on a version
steps.problem: Two bidders read the same current price and both submit a higher amount. With read, check and insert as separate steps, both succeed, and the rule that a bid must beat the current price is not enforced.
steps.fix: Keep one row per auction in a store that supports conditional writes: current price, leader, end time, and a version number. A bid carries the version the bidder saw. The API applies it with a single statement that only succeeds if the version is still the same, and increments the version. If the update matches no row, someone else got in first, so the API re-reads the row and either retries the bid against the new price or tells the bidder they have been outbid. Auctions are independent, so the data is partitioned by auction id and a hot auction only contends with itself.
steps.tradeoff: Correctness without long locks, and a loser finds out immediately. On a very hot auction many attempts fail and retry, so the retries must be bounded and use a short backoff. A write on one row is serial, which is acceptable because one auction rarely needs more than a few hundred bids per second.

steps.title: Rank by highest bid and bid on the bidder's behalf
steps.problem: Bidders do not want to sit at the screen raising their bid by one step. And the ordering of bids must be exact: the highest bid wins, and between equal bids the earlier one wins.
steps.fix: A bid is a maximum the bidder will pay. The proxy bidding service keeps only the leader's maximum, and when a new bid arrives it decides inside the same conditional write. If the new maximum is higher, the new bidder leads and the price becomes the old maximum plus one increment, capped at the new maximum. If it is not higher, the leader stays and the price rises to the challenger's maximum plus one increment, capped at the leader's maximum. Equal maximums go to the earlier bid. Every accepted bid is also appended to a bid ledger with its server time and sequence number, indexed by auction and amount.
steps.tradeoff: The price is the lowest one that still wins, bidders can set and forget, and the ordering is deterministic. The leader's maximum is a secret that must never reach the clients or the push channel, and the logic must handle the odd cases, such as the leader raising their own maximum, which does not change the price.

steps.title: Extend the end time when someone bids late
steps.problem: A bidder who places a bid one second before the end wins because the other bidder cannot react. That rewards fast scripts and network luck rather than how much the item is worth to people.
steps.fix: The auction row holds an end time. If a bid is accepted when less than the window remains, for example two minutes, the same conditional write moves the end time to the bid time plus the window. The bid and the new end time commit together, using the server's clock only. A close scheduler keeps the auctions ordered by end time and re-arms the one that moved. A cap on the number of extensions, or a final hard stop, stops an auction from running for ever.
steps.tradeoff: The auction ends only when real competition stops, and the final price is usually higher. The end time is no longer fixed, which surprises some sellers and bidders and needs clear messages. Because the scheduler can fire for an old end time, the close step must re-check the end time under the same version.

steps.title: Fan out each change to the watchers
steps.problem: Thousands of people watch the same hot auction. If each one polls the database, the read load lands on exactly the rows that are being written the most.
steps.fix: After a bid commits, the ledger publishes a bid event to a topic (a named channel that subscribers listen to) for that auction. A fleet of push gateways holds the watchers' connections, subscribes to the topics of the auctions its clients are looking at, and sends the new price, leader and end time. In the last seconds many bids arrive per second, so each gateway batches to the latest state every few hundred milliseconds instead of sending every bid. A new watcher gets a snapshot read from a cache, then the changes after it, numbered by version so a gap or reorder is detected and repaired by fetching the snapshot again.
steps.tradeoff: Watchers see changes almost at once and the database never sees them. Batching means a watcher can skip an intermediate price, which is fine because only the latest state matters. The bid is confirmed to the bidder from the write itself, never from the push, so a lost push message costs nothing but a refresh.

steps.title: Close each auction exactly once
steps.problem: At the end time the system must pick a winner, charge them and create an order. A timer that fires twice, a worker that crashes halfway, or a bid that arrives at the same moment must not produce two orders, no order, or a different winner.
steps.fix: The scheduler hands due auctions to close workers through a queue, which can deliver a job more than once. The worker closes with one conditional write: set the state from open to closed only if the version and the end time are the ones it read and the end time has passed. Only one worker wins that write. The order is created with the auction id as its idempotency key (a unique id, so a repeated request acts once), in the same transaction or through an outbox (a table row saved with the change and sent on afterwards), so a repeat finds the existing order. A sweeper looks for auctions past their end that are still open and re-enqueues them, so a missed timer costs seconds, not an auction.
steps.tradeoff: At-least-once delivery with an idempotent effect behaves as exactly once, and every failure is repaired by simply running the job again. It needs a unique key and a stored state for every auction, and a payment charge needs its own idempotency key towards the payment provider.

steps.title: Keep it fair and keep the evidence
steps.problem: Bots, shill accounts that bid up their own seller's items, and disputes after the fact all damage trust. When someone says they were outbid unfairly, the system must be able to prove what happened.
steps.fix: The ledger is append-only: each entry has the bid, the version, the server time, the price after it and a hash of the previous entry, so editing or removing one breaks the chain. The auction's state can be rebuilt by replaying the ledger. Fair-play checks run beside the bid path: rate limits per account and per device, a rule that sellers and linked accounts cannot bid, and detection of patterns such as the same two accounts raising each other. Suspicious bids are flagged for review rather than blocked in the hot path, and everything uses the server clock, never the client's.
steps.tradeoff: Disputes can be answered from facts, and the same rules apply to everyone. The ledger grows without end and must be archived, detection produces false positives that need a human, and checks must stay out of the latency of the bid itself.

failures.scenario: Two bids for the same auction arrive in the same millisecond
failures.impact: Both bidders saw the same price. If both are accepted, the price and the leader depend on which write lands last.
failures.answer: Both carry the same version, so only one conditional write succeeds. The other gets a conflict, re-reads the new price and is applied again if it still beats it, or rejected as too low with a clear message. Retries are limited to a few attempts with a short random delay, so a hot auction does not spin.

failures.scenario: The close job is delivered twice, or the worker crashes after charging
failures.impact: The winner is charged twice, or the auction is marked closed with no order.
failures.answer: The close is a single conditional write from open to closed, so a second delivery finds the auction already closed and stops. The order and the charge both use the auction id as an idempotency key, and the order is written together with the state change or through an outbox. The sweeper re-enqueues any auction that is past its end and still open, so a crash is repaired by running the job again.

failures.scenario: A popular item gets 50,000 watchers and a bid war in its last minute
failures.impact: Every bid would be sent 50,000 times, and the gateways and the row both come under pressure.
failures.answer: Pushes are batched so that each watcher gets at most a few updates per second, and carry only the latest state with its version. Gateways subscribe to the auction's topic once and share it among their clients. Bids themselves are limited per account, and the hot auction's row writes stay on its own partition, so other auctions are unaffected.

failures.scenario: A server's clock is a few seconds off
failures.impact: A bid is accepted after the end, or refused before it, and the extension window starts at the wrong moment.
failures.answer: Only one source of time decides: the database timestamp inside the same conditional write that accepts the bid. Clients show a countdown but never decide anything with it. Application servers keep their clocks synchronised and are monitored for drift, and a bid within a small grace period of the end is judged by the stored end time and nothing else.

failures.scenario: A seller's second account bids their own item up
failures.impact: Honest bidders pay more than the item is worth, and trust in the site falls.
failures.answer: Fair-play checks compare accounts by device, payment method and address, block the seller and linked accounts from bidding, and flag pairs that raise each other repeatedly. The append-only ledger lets reviewers replay the auction, void the shill bids and recompute the price, and the bidders who were affected are told.

alternatives.title: How to stop two bids from both winning

options.name: Optimistic version check
options.pro: No locks held, the loser knows at once, and it fits any store with conditional writes
options.con: Retries pile up on a very hot auction

options.name: Row lock around the bid
options.con: Locks are held across network calls, and a stuck client can block everyone

options.name: One single-writer queue per auction
options.pro: No conflicts at all, since bids are applied one at a time in order
options.con: Needs routing by auction, ordering guarantees and failover of the writer

alternatives.pick: A version check on the auction row. Move a very hot auction to a single writer if retries become the bottleneck.

alternatives.title: How to end an auction

options.name: Hard end time
options.con: Rewards sniping and often ends below what bidders would pay

options.name: Soft close with extensions
options.pro: Everyone has time to answer, and the price reflects real demand
options.con: No fixed finish, so a cap and clear messages are needed

options.name: Sealed bids
options.pro: No sniping, since nobody sees the others
options.con: A different product, with no live excitement and no watchers to serve

alternatives.pick: Soft close with a window of a couple of minutes and a cap on the number of extensions.

options.name: Open ascending with proxy bidding
options.pro: The winner pays one step over the runner-up, and bidders can set and forget
options.con: The leader's maximum must be kept secret and the logic is more subtle

options.name: Plain highest bid, no proxy
options.con: Bidders must stay at the screen and guess

options.name: Pay what you bid
options.con: Bidders shade their bids, and rational play is more complicated

alternatives.title: How watchers get updates

options.name: Polling
options.pro: Simple, with no connections to keep
options.con: Load is highest on the hottest auctions, and updates arrive late

options.name: WebSocket or server-sent events
options.pro: Updates arrive within a second and the database is not involved
options.con: Many open connections to manage, and clients need resync logic

alternatives.pick: Push through gateways, with a polling fallback.

roles.description: People who bid and people who follow an auction.

roles.description: The bid API and the push gateway.

roles.label: Events and timers
roles.description: Bid events and the close scheduler.

quiz.question: An auction page reads the highest bid, checks that the new amount is higher, and inserts a row, as three separate steps. At the same instant two bidders who both saw a price of 100 submit 110 and 120. Both inserts succeed. What is the right fix?
options: Add a unique index on (auction, amount), so two bids of the same amount cannot both be stored and the later insert is rejected by the database itself.
Hold a row lock on the auction from the moment a bidder opens the bid form until the bid is submitted, so only one bidder at a time can be mid-bid and others wait.
Keep a version on the auction row and apply each bid as one conditional write that succeeds only if the version is unchanged, so a loser retries.
Move the bids table to a larger database instance so the read, check and insert finish faster and the window for a clash becomes tiny.
quiz.explanation: The flaw is that the check and the write are separate, so both bidders pass the check against the same price. A conditional write on a version makes them one atomic step. A unique index on amount does not help because 110 and 120 are different values, a bigger machine only narrows the race, and a lock held while a form is open lets one idle bidder block everyone.

quiz.question: A hot auction has 50,000 watchers and receives about 20 bids per second in its last minute. Sending every bid to every watcher would mean 1,000,000 messages per second. The goal is to stay near 100,000 messages per second while every watcher still ends on the true final price. Which design does that?
options: Push gateways send each watcher the latest state (price, leader, end time, version) every 500 ms, so a watcher may skip prices but ends on the current one.
Drop 9 out of every 10 bid events at random before they reach the gateways, which cuts the load to about 100,000 messages per second for this auction.
Have every watcher poll the auction row every 500 ms, which also gives about 100,000 requests per second and needs no push infrastructure or fan-out service at all.
Send every bid event, but only to the 5,000 watchers who have placed a bid on this auction before, since they care about price changes.
quiz.explanation: Only the latest state matters to a watcher, so a snapshot every 500 ms means 2 updates per second per watcher, or 100,000 per second, and the last one is always the real price. Random dropping can lose the final event and leave a watcher on a stale price. Polling puts the same rate onto the hottest row in the database, and sending only to past bidders leaves the other watchers on a stale price.

quiz.question: Close jobs are delivered at least once, and a job can fire for an end time that a late bid has since extended. Worker A closes auction 77, creates the order, then crashes before it acknowledges, so worker B receives the same job. How should closing work to get one winner and one order?
options: Take a distributed lock on the auction id with a 30 second TTL before closing, so only the current lock holder can run the close logic for that auction, one at a time.
Switch the queue to its exactly-once delivery mode, so the close job reaches a single worker only and the order step needs no protection of its own.
Run one close worker on one machine and restart it after a crash, so duplicates cannot happen because no two workers ever see the same job.
Close with one conditional write from open to closed that checks version, end time and the clock, and key the order by its auction id.
quiz.explanation: A conditional write on the auction state makes the second delivery and the stale timer harmless, and the idempotency key on the order covers a crash between the two steps. A lock with a TTL can expire during a pause and does not remember that the auction is already closed. Queue-level exactly-once cannot cover a worker that crashes after its side effects, and a single worker is a single point of failure that still re-reads a half-finished job.
